system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Threshold point: the "[STANDARD]" labels and "Reviewer Efficiency Note"

The Seller has tagged almost every material position "[STANDARD]". Its note says these were "reviewed and cleared by both sides", that we should "focus only on anything marked [OPEN]", and that we have "already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package."

**Recommendation:** Do not accept this framing.
- No item in the package is marked [OPEN]. Following the note would mean reviewing nothing.
- The labels are the Seller's own characterisation in its own draft. They are not an agreed issues list.
- The Seller's own Disclosure Letter contradicts several "[STANDARD]" items. For example, Bluefen is said to be "addressed", but Disclosure Letter para 2 confirms there is no consent.
- I have no record that Wattlebridge agreed to the disclosure framework or the limitation package. Please confirm internally whether anything was conceded in earlier calls or term sheets.
- Our cover response should state expressly that all positions remain open and that the Buyer does not accept the [STANDARD] designations.

I have reviewed every item on its merits below, in rough order of priority.

---

## Tier 1: Critical issues (deal-protection or value-at-risk)

### 1. Fundamental warranties pushed into the general cap and time limit
**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties are subject to the 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) and the 18-month time limit, "for administrative simplicity".

**Why it matters:** Title is what we are paying AUD 24m for. If the Seller does not own 100% of the shares unencumbered, a AUD 4.8m cap leaves us recovering only 20% of the price. Combined with the 18-month bar, a title defect found in year two would be unrecoverable.

**Push back:**
- Title and capacity warranties should be capped at 100% of the price.
- Claims should be allowed for at least 6 years, consistent with the NSW *Limitation Act 1969* period for contract, or 12 years if the SPA is executed as a deed.
- The de minimis and basket should not apply to these warranties.

### 2. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 12.3 / 13 / 20.5)
**Seller position:** All limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise. The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to Claims "of any nature".

**Why it matters:** This would sweep in specific indemnities, tax claims, covenant breaches, leakage and price-adjustment claims, and potentially fraud. It also tries to shut out misleading or deceptive conduct claims under s18 of the Australian Consumer Law. Australian courts will not let a party exclude liability for its own fraud. Even so, a broadly drafted non-reliance clause can significantly weaken an ACL or misrepresentation claim on the evidence.

**Push back:** Invert the default so limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims. Expressly carve out:
- fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller or its representatives;
- Fundamental and Tax Warranties, which should have their own cap and period;
- all specific indemnities (Ironquay, DD-006, bonuses, Riverlark);
- covenant breaches, leakage and price-adjustment or completion-accounts amounts.

Non-reliance should be limited to matters outside the Warranties and Disclosure Letter, and should not cover fraud.

### 3. Riverlark facility (~AUD 3.2m): release "following Completion"
**Seller position:** A release will be provided after Completion. Disclosure Letter para 3 confirms the facility is unpaid and no discharge is in hand.

**Why it matters:** The deal is debt-free/cash-free. A post-Completion release means:
- we pay the full price while the Company remains indebted and encumbered;
- the change-control clause (8.1) may trigger a default on Completion;
- we depend on the Seller's post-Completion goodwill to procure the release.

The Riverlark security may also extend to the shares being sold, which must be checked.

**Push back:** Make discharge a Completion deliverable:
- a payoff letter from Riverlark stating the exact payoff amount and confirming release on receipt;
- a deed of release covering all security and guarantees;
- authority to register PPSR financing change statements.

The payoff amount should be paid directly to Riverlark out of the price through the funds flow and treated as Debt in the price mechanics. We should also add a specific indemnity for any residual Riverlark liability, including break costs and default interest.

### 4. Bluefen consent (~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of FY26 revenue)
**Seller position:** "Addressed". The Seller offers reasonable endeavours, with the condition treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. Disclosure Letter para 2, however, confirms there is no final consent and no evidence that the clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied.

**Why it matters:** Losing the Company's largest customer would fundamentally change its value. "Written consent" alone could be conditional, partial, revocable, or tied to unmet 11.3 conditions. Reasonable endeavours is a weak obligation.

**Push back:**
- The condition precedent should require an unconditional written consent from Bluefen, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably. All clause 11.3 conditions must be satisfied or waived by Bluefen, and the consent must not be withdrawn before Completion.
- The Seller should use best (or all reasonable) endeavours, keep the Buyer informed and give it a right to review communications with Bluefen.
- The condition should be waivable only by the Buyer, with a long-stop date and a Buyer termination right.
- Consider a price adjustment or escrow if Bluefen gives consent on changed commercial terms.
- We need the full text of DD-002 clauses 11.2–11.3 to settle the drafting. I have only the Seller's summary.

### 5. Disclosure: general disclosure of the data room and public records (Schedule 7 / Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2)
**Why it matters:** Disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room, accounts, statutory registers and public records hollows out the warranties. Any matter buried anywhere in the data room would defeat a claim. The data room is cut off at 22 September 2026, six weeks ago, with no index attached.

**Push back:**
- Delete general disclosure. Only specific disclosures in the Disclosure Letter should qualify warranties.
- Each disclosure must be fair: sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and financial effect of the matter. Cross-referencing a document is not enough.
- If any data-room disclosure is conceded, it should be limited to documents in an agreed index, initialled and attached, and still subject to the fair-disclosure standard.
- Exclude public records, or limit them to specified searches on specified dates.
- Specific disclosures should not qualify Fundamental Warranties or specific indemnities.
- Paragraph 1.4 (no admission) is acceptable in principle. It must not be read as diluting the specific disclosures.

### 6. Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3): anti-sandbagging
**Seller position:** No claim for any matter known to the Buyer or its advisers, "including any matter discoverable" from the data room or public records.

**Why it matters:** This introduces constructive knowledge through "discoverable" and imputes knowledge across all our advisers. Together with general disclosure, it would make the warranty package close to illusory. It also penalises us for doing due diligence.

**Push back:** Replace it with a clause stating that the Buyer's knowledge, actual or constructive, does not affect any claim or reduce any recoverable loss. If the Seller resists, the fallback is to limit it to the actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals of matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter. Constructive knowledge and adviser knowledge should be excluded in all cases.

---

## Tier 2: Specific liabilities needing indemnities or price treatment

### 7. DD-005 closing bonuses (AUD 420,000 plus on-costs) missing from the funds flow
**Seller position:** The bonuses are "a matter for the Seller" and not itemised.

**Why it matters:** The employer is the Company, so after Completion the liability sits with an entity we own. On top of the AUD 420k there will likely be:
- PAYG withholding;
- superannuation guarantee (12% from 1 July 2025, if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings);
- NSW payroll tax;
- workers compensation premium impact.

The Disclosure Letter is silent on all of these. The funds flow therefore understates what the Company owes.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses and all on-costs as Debt or Transaction Expenses, deducted from the price.
- Itemise them in the funds flow, with the Company paying through payroll at or immediately after Completion, funded from the Seller's proceeds.
- Add a specific indemnity uncapped by the general regime, covering the bonuses, on-costs, penalties, and any claims from employees who argue they met the conditions.
- Request the bonus letters to check the continued-employment and Completion conditions.

### 8. Ironquay / SOW3 IP (cl 11.1)
**Seller position:** The indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment is "adequate".

**Why it matters:** Under DD-004 clause 7.3, IP in the SOW3 Project Materials transfers only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open, and there is no receipt or confirmatory assignment. Ironquay may still own the IP. An indemnity covering only the payment ignores the larger risks: injunction, infringement claims, licence fees, and the cost of re-developing or replacing the materials.

**Push back:**
- **Completion deliverables:** evidence that the AUD 180k has been paid (Ironquay's written confirmation of receipt, not internal records), plus an executed confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay, with moral rights consents where relevant.
- **Fallback:** if those cannot be delivered before Completion, deduct the AUD 180k as Debt and hold an escrow.
- **Broader indemnity:** in all cases, a specific indemnity covering ownership defects, third-party claims, lost use and remediation costs, outside the general cap, basket and time limit.
- **IP warranties:** these should not be "settled under the general regime". Seek a longer period, and treat core IP ownership as close to fundamental.

### 9. DD-006 export and privacy incident (~1,240 records)
**Seller position:** A "preliminary operational matter", not expected to be material.

**Why it matters:**
- A download link containing personal information was sent to an unintended external address. Access, scope and notification are all undetermined.
- Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must take reasonable steps to assess it within 30 days (s 26WH). If the incident predates 22 September, that window may already have passed. Late or no notification is itself a compliance risk.
- Exposure includes OAIC investigation, civil penalties under the strengthened 2022 and 2024 penalty regime, notification and remediation costs, and claims by affected individuals, potentially including the statutory privacy tort.
- The Seller's view that the matter is "not expected to be material" is unsupported by its own disclosure.

**Push back:**
- Require an updated investigation or forensic report before signing, or at least before Completion.
- Require the Company's documented NDB assessment and notification decision. Any decision should be taken before Completion, in consultation with the Buyer.
- Add a pre-Completion covenant to manage the incident in consultation with the Buyer.
- Add a specific indemnity for all losses arising from the incident, uncapped by the general regime, with an extended time limit and not qualified by disclosure.
- Confirm whether the Company's cyber insurance has been notified.

### 10. Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)
**Seller position:** "Ordinary-course operating costs."

**Why it matters:** Three "related" renewals of identical value, which the Disclosure Letter itself says should be read together, raise several questions:
- Was the commitment split to stay under a pre-Completion conduct-of-business threshold or an internal approval threshold?
- Is "related" a reference to a related party of the Seller? If so, payments may be leakage.
- Are the contracts terminable, and are the costs accrued?

The Disclosure Letter expressly does not say whether the renewals are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Push back:**
- Request the contracts (DD-008 and DD-011) and confirm whether Sandbar is related to the Seller.
- If related-party, treat payments as leakage, or require termination before Completion.
- Aggregate related contracts when applying conduct-of-business thresholds, so that future splitting is caught.
- Require Buyer consent for any further renewals.
- Seek a warranty that the renewals were entered on arm's-length, ordinary-course terms.
- Depending on the answers, seek a price adjustment or termination at the Seller's cost.

---

## Tier 3: Title, contracts and verification

### 11. Title (DD-012)
**Seller position:** Title is "evidenced" by the share register.

**Why it matters:** A self-maintained register is not sufficient. Disclosure Letter para 10 itself notes that the Buyer has not completed its own verification.

**Push back:**
- Complete our own verification: ASIC company extract, constitution, issue history, any options, convertibles or rights to shares, and a PPSR search against the Seller and the Company. That search should specifically check whether Riverlark or anyone else holds security over the shares.
- Title should be a Fundamental Warranty (see item 1).
- **Completion deliverables:** signed share transfer forms, original share certificates or a lost-certificate indemnity, waivers of any pre-emption rights, releases of any share security, and director resignations and appointments.

### 12. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
The Seller has characterised these provisions in its own favour:
- the lease requires notification only, not landlord consent;
- the Mossvale restriction on assignment does not cover a share sale.

**Push back:**
- Review both provisions ourselves. Many contracts deem a change of control to be an assignment.
- Make the lease notice a Completion deliverable, or an agreed post-Completion step.
- If Mossvale's definition of assignment captures a change of control, add it to the consents condition precedent.
- Add a warranty that no material contract contains a change-of-control provision other than those specifically listed.

---

## Tier 4: General limitation package (negotiable, but improve)

| Item | Seller | Recommended Buyer position |
|---|---|---|
| General cap | 20% (AUD 4.8m) | Acceptable range, but seek 30–50% absent W&I. Carve-outs per item 2 are essential. |
| De minimis | AUD 25k | Lower to ~AUD 10–15k. Aggregate related claims for the de minimis. |
| Basket | AUD 250k, excess only | Tipping basket (recover from dollar one once exceeded). Consider ~AUD 120–180k. |
| General time limit | 18 months | 24 months, or at least two audit cycles. |
| Tax warranties / indemnity | General regime | Cap at 100% of price. Allow claims until ~3 months after the ATO amendment period expires (typically 4–5 years). |
| IP warranties | General regime | Extended period (e.g. 3 years). Core ownership treated as near-fundamental. |
| Specific indemnities | Caught by general regime | Outside the cap, basket, de minimis and disclosure. Own time limits. |

Consider W&I insurance. It can make a lower Seller cap tolerable, but only if the known issues (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-006, bonuses) are covered by specific indemnities and escrow, because insurers will exclude them as known matters.

---

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Reject the [STANDARD] / "already accepted" framing.** Confirm internally that nothing was conceded, and state in writing that all positions remain open.
2. **Fundamental warranties:** cap at 100% of the price with a 6+ year time limit, excluded from the de minimis and basket.
3. **Carve-outs from all limitations:** fraud, Fundamental and Tax Warranties, specific indemnities, covenants and leakage. Narrow the non-reliance clause.
4. **Riverlark:** payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR releases as Completion deliverables, paid from the price as Debt.
5. **Bluefen:** an unconditional consent condition, with clause 11.3 conditions satisfied, best endeavours, a Buyer-only waiver, a long-stop date and a termination right.
6. **Disclosure:** specific and fair disclosure only. Delete general data-room and public-record disclosure.
7. **Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3):** replace with a pro-sandbagging clause, or at minimum actual knowledge of named individuals only.
8. **DD-005 bonuses:** AUD 420k plus PAYG, super and payroll tax deducted as Debt or Transaction Expenses, itemised in the funds flow and backed by a specific indemnity.
9. **Ironquay:** payment confirmation and a confirmatory IP assignment at Completion, plus a broad specific indemnity, with an escrow or price deduction as fallback.
10. **DD-006:** a current forensic report and NDB assessment, a pre-Completion management covenant, and a specific uncapped indemnity.
11. **Sandbar:** obtain the contracts, test for related-party status and threshold-splitting, then treat as leakage or require termination or Buyer consent.
12. **Title, lease and Mossvale:** independent verification, Completion deliverables, and a change-of-control warranty.
13. **General package:** a tipping basket, a lower de minimis, a 24-month general period, and separate tax and IP regimes. Consider W&I insurance.

**Information to request from the Seller:**
- full text of DD-002 cl 11.2–11.3, DD-003 cl 8.1 and 9.2, DD-004 cl 7.3, DD-007 and DD-009;
- the bonus letters;
- the Sandbar contracts and any relationship between Sandbar and the Seller;
- the DD-006 incident timeline and investigation file;
- an updated data-room index;
- confirmation of the price mechanism (locked box or completion accounts), so that leakage and Debt definitions can be settled.

I can prepare a mark-up of the relevant clauses or an issues-list response to Seller's counsel if helpful.
=== END ADVICE ===
